title: Teaching on Purpose #20 Checking for Understanding
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: In this installment of his Chiltern Learning Trust series, Adam Kohlbeck recaps a conversation with Yamina Bibi about checking for understanding, building on earlier episodes on show-me boards, no opt out and hinge questions. The first theme is that every one of those techniques is only as good as the multiple choice question beneath it, and that the quality of a question lives in its plausible distractors. Drawing on Daisy Christodoulou and Stuart Kime, he lists principles such as avoiding negative phrasing and complex vocabulary and aiming for mutually exclusive distractors that each reveal a distinct misconception. The second theme is Doug Lemov's Right is Right, which holds out for the all the way right answer, and he adds that it suits probing individual pupils but not quick whole-class reads. He closes by arguing that departments should use meeting time to write questions together and plan how they will check understanding alongside what they will teach.
points: A multiple choice question with two obviously wrong options gives a guessing pupil a 50/50 chance, so a healthy-looking set of correct answers can hide real misunderstanding.
The most useful habit is to scan the room for the wrong answers rather than the right ones, because the distractors chosen point to the misconception to reteach.
Right is Right means holding out for the complete answer through probing, bringing in other pupils, or rephrasing the question, and it is a high-expectations move rather than a rejection of effort.
Right is Right fits developing one pupil's response, not whole-class checks where the goal is a fast, accurate read of the room.
Writing strong questions is better done collaboratively in department time, and planning how to check understanding should sit beside planning the content.
quotes: The heart of a strong multiple choice question is its plausible distractors. Every wrong answer should be one that a pupil might realistically choose, and each one should tell us something specific about what they have misunderstood.
I would go as far as to say that a poorly designed multiple choice question is not just a missed opportunity. It is a risk to learning, because it hides exactly the thing it was designed to reveal.
The way I like to think about it is that we are not checking whether pupils have understood. We are checking what they have understood.
But standing there, it struck me that the incorrect answers were far more useful. They were the ones that told me which misconception I needed to go back and address.
The idea is that we hold out for the all the way right answer rather than accepting one that is partially correct. It is a question of high expectations.
Right is Right comes into its own when the purpose is to develop a response, to get a pupil to justify their thinking, refine their language and show the precise extent of what they have understood.
If our planning is only about content coverage, we will find ourselves making it up in the moment.
